title: The third truth
hookLine: the fading away and ending of that same craving: relief is possible

cards: You've carried the grocery bags up three flights of stairs. The handles have cut red lines into your fingers.
You get the door open, swing the bags onto the counter, and there it is: a rush of lightness in your arms, so strong you almost laugh. Nothing was added. Something was put down.
The Buddha used almost exactly this picture, a man setting down a heavy load, to explain the truth that turns the whole teaching from a diagnosis into good news.

teach.b: The third truth is nirodha: stopping, ending, cessation.

In the first sermon the Buddha describes it as the complete fading away and ending of that very craving: giving it up, letting it go, being free of it, no longer leaning on it. Notice those words, that very craving.
The third truth doesn't promise that pain will never touch your body or that loss will skip your house. It says the thirst that turns pain into suffering can end.

A short sutta in the Connected Discourses, called the Burden, lays it out like the stairs. The burden is the five heaps that make up a person. The one who carries it is the person, so-and-so, of such a family.
Picking the burden up is craving. Setting it down is the ending of craving.
He closes with a little verse: taking up the burden is suffering in the world, and putting it down is happiness.
So the relief doesn't come from getting what we want, or getting away from what we don't. It comes from the thirst itself going quiet.
Some teachers point to tiny previews: the moment after an argument when the need to win drops away, the night the phone stays face down and sleep comes.
What the full ending is like, the suttas mostly describe by what's absent, and that's tomorrow. Today's point is simpler. The chain isn't welded shut.

how: Buddhists recite the third truth as part of the four noble truths, and some meditation teachers point students to brief moments when craving falls quiet as small tastes of what the third truth describes.

o: a rule that forbids all desire
a calm that numbs every feeling

games.q: match the pieces of the burden sutta.

s: the third truth promises that pain will never touch you again
it says the craving that drives dukkha can end; the body still ages and aches.
in the Burden sutta, setting the burden down is the ending of craving
picking it up is craving; setting it down is its ending.
it's the Pali word for cessation, the third truth.

games.q: in the Burden sutta, a man is carrying a heavy load. what does the Buddha say picking up the load stands for?
games.why: picking up the burden is craving, and setting it down is the ending of craving; the verse says taking it up is suffering and putting it down is happiness.

practice: For a little while, don't want the next breath to be better than this one, or the sit to end, or to go well. If a want appears, notice it, and set it down like a bag on a counter.
Look for even one second where nothing is being reached for; you don't have to make it last.

wordCard.voice: Nirodha. Ending, cessation: the third noble truth, which says that craving, and the dukkha it drives, can fade away and stop.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit nirodha: stopping, cessation; the third noble truth.

carryVoice: Your line: it can stop. Even a second of craving letting go is a small piece of the third truth. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: SN 56.11 (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta), the third noble truth
